title: perf-incident-2026-02-hotfix-validation
content:
Summary:

On 2026-02-20 at ~10:17 UTC we observed a rapid degradation in serving runtime latency across the hosted API fleet affecting multi-tenant customers. The degradation manifested as p95 latency spikes from a steady ~240ms to >980ms and resulted in a 14-minute window of SLO misses for the p95 < 500ms objective. The root cause was a regression in kernel selection / compilation behavior introduced by runtime change commit a1f3c9 (merged via PR #482) combined with KV cache eviction behavior under memory pressure.

Impact:
- Duration: ~10:17 - 10:31 UTC (14 minutes)
- Scope: ~22% of hosted capacity (regions us-west2 / us-east4 routing buckets)
- Customers impacted: multiple paying customers with strict latency SLOs; two customers (AcmeAI, FinQ) escalated via CSMs during the incident.
- Symptoms: sudden p50/p95/p99 jumps, queue length growth on async batcher, error budget burn for p95. No increase in 5xx error rate observed.

Timeline (high level):
- 10:16 UTC - internal alerts for p95 crossing 600ms
- 10:17 UTC - automated routing fallback triggered for some traffic patterns; alerts escalate to on-call eng-serving-runtime
- 10:20 UTC - initial mitigation: increase routing to Dedicated fallback tier for critical customers; immediate short-term relief for ~30% of impacted requests
- 10:22 UTC - profiling artifacts collected (heap/alloc/cpu traces) and uploaded to S3
- 10:25 UTC - rolling revert of PR #482 started for canary hosts
- 10:29 UTC - canary hosts show latency return to baseline; gradual rollout of revert to remaining hosts
- 10:31 UTC - metrics back to pre-incident baselines; monitoring remained stable thereafter

Initial Detection & Escalation Details:
- Detection via p95 latency alert rule (threshold 500ms sustained for 2m) from Grafana.
- Pager on-call (Diego Ramirez) paged and created INF-1234; engaged Priya (SRE) and Maya (solutions).
- CSMs notified customers with public-facing incident note and a brief postmortem promise.

Root Cause Analysis (summary):
- Regression introduced in runtime commit a1f3c9 (kernel selection logic) changed the heuristic that chooses between precompiled kernels (FlashAttention-v2 optimized) and a new fallback JIT path intended for uncommon sequence-lengths. Under normal load the JIT path is rarely used; the commit unintentionally increased the JIT selection probability by roughly 3-4x for certain sequence length distributions.
- At high concurrency and when memory fragmentation increased (we were simultaneously experiencing higher-than-average small-batch traffic), the JIT path triggered on-demand kernel compilation. The compilation is CPU-heavy and serialized per-model, which caused request queueing inside the batcher and increased end-to-end latency.
- Contributing factor: KV cache eviction policy was more aggressive in the same release (tuned to reduce memory for underutilized models). This increased cold cache misses for repeated short-context requests, which partially amplified CPU work per request.
- Not a cause: no unexpected hardware failures, no network partitions, and 5xx rate stayed flat; therefore the root cause is primarily software-level scheduling/compilation and memory policy interaction.

Evidence collected:
- Flame graphs from canary hosts (s3://redwood-profiles/2026-02-20/alloc-profile-heap.pb) showing high time in kernel JIT compile path (compile_kernel()) during incident window.
- Grafana: batcher-queue-length metric spiking with average queue depth increasing from 1.1 to 5.8 in affected buckets.
- Latency histograms: sudden mass shift in p95/p99 corresponding to compilation windows.
- Traces: sampled traces show single-request wait time correlated to waiting on compilation mutex.

Profiling & Benchmarks (what we ran to reproduce/validate):
- Local perf harness: replayed production traffic distribution (sequence length histogram, batch sizes) against two runtime builds (pre-commit and post-commit). Post-commit showed 2.6x higher 95th latency under concurrency=64.
- Microbenchmark: kernel compile time averaged ~180ms per compile for typical attention kernels at our model quantization.
- Memory pressure test: synthetic driver triggered KV cache churn; combination with JIT path reproduced queue growth reliably.

Immediate Mitigation / Hotfix Applied:
- Rollback of PR #482 (revert commit a1f3c9) deployed to canary fleet at 10:25 UTC and rolled to all hosts by 10:31 UTC. This restored previous kernel selection heuristic.
- Adjusted autoscaler to temporarily add capacity to impacted routing buckets while rollback rolled through to prevent further SLO erosion.
- Temporary KV cache tune: increased cache size + less aggressive eviction for 30 minutes during rollback windows.

Hotfix Validation Steps (what we did to confirm fix):
1) Canary synthetic replay: run production traffic replay on canaries running revert build and measure p95/p99 for 30 minutes. Observed latency drop to baseline (p95 back to ~230ms).
2) End-to-end blackbox tests: internal e2e harness (1000 requests across sequence lengths) passed with p95 < 400ms.
3) Gradual traffic ramp: moved 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% traffic off fallback and back to normal routing, monitoring p95/p99 and queue depth during each step.
4) Post-rollout profiling: re-captured allocation and CPU profiles to ensure no lingering compile hotspots.
5) Customer validation: CSMs confirmed improvement for reported customers; we provided isolated traces to their SREs.

Postmortem Findings / Lessons Learned:
- Hot code-path changes that alter kernel selection heuristics must have an automated microbenchmark gate that simulates high-concurrency JIT compile scenarios (we lacked this in CI).
- Batcher queue depth and compile locks are a critical single point that can amplify minor heuristics regressions; add additional observability (compile-rate, per-model compilation mutex wait time) to alert before user-visible SLOs are hit.
- KV cache tuning changes should be tested in combination with serving runtime changes - not in isolation - because interaction effects are non-linear.
- Revert was the correct immediate action; however, we should have a pre-approved quick rollback runbook for kernel-level changes.

Action Items (owner / due):
- Add a microbenchmark job in CI to simulate JIT compile pressure (owner: Priya Kapoor, due: 2026-03-12).
- Instrument compile mutex wait time and per-model compile-rate in Prometheus/Grafana and create alerts for sustained increases (owner: Diego Ramirez, due: 2026-03-05).
- Create a combined test matrix for KV cache policy vs kernel selection heuristics (owner: Liam O'Neill, due: 2026-03-19).
- Formalize a faster rollback runbook for binary/kernel selection changes and ensure on-call training (owner: Maya Patel, due: 2026-03-01).
- Deliver customer-facing postmortem note to impacted customers with a timeline and remediation steps (owner: CSM team, support: Avery Chen, due: 2026-02-29).

Customer Escalation Notes:
- Tickets: INF-1234 (engineering incident), CS-2026-02-Acme (AcmeAI escalation), CS-2026-02-FinQ (FinQ escalation).
- AcmeAI reported a critical user-facing slowdown at 10:18 UTC; provided them an initial mitigation note and invited them to the postmortem review.
- FinQ required an SLA credit assessment; finance/legal looped in after postmortem review.

Open Questions / Follow-ups:
- Do we need a global guardrail that disables on-demand JIT compilation for hosted API customers unless explicit opt-in is provided? (security/ops implication)
- How much headroom should we keep for KV caches per-host to avoid these interactions at scale?
- Should we invest in background pre-compilation for common sequence-lengths to avoid runtime JIT spikes?

Appendix (short commands / artifacts):
- Repro harness: tools/perf/replay --trace s3://prod-traces/2026-02-20/ --build post-commit
- Profile artifacts: s3://redwood-profiles/2026-02-20/alloc-profile-heap.pb
- PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482 (reverted)

Notes to self / informal:
- We were lucky this hit a routing bucket with healthy fallback capacity; could have been much worse if Dedicated pools were at 100% commit.
- Need to loop in product-hosted-api to set stricter gates for runtime changes that affect kernel selection.

Prepared by: Avery Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
Reviewers: Diego Ramirez, Priya Kapoor, Liam O'Neill

Status: final.
